title: Scatter Plots and Patterns
tagline: Two variables, one plot. You'll see clusters, lines, curves, and weirdos.
what_it_is: A scatter plot puts one variable on the x‑axis, another on the y‑axis. Each point is one observation. The pattern tells you the relationship. Linear: points form a line. Nonlinear: they form a curve. Clusters: separate groups. Outliers: lonely points far from the crowd. Scatter plots are the workhorse of bivariate EDA.
key_points: Linear pattern = straight line. Positive slope (up right) or negative (down right).
Nonlinear = curved. Examples: U‑shape, exponential growth, logarithmic.
Clusters = distinct groups. May need separate models per cluster.
Outliers = extreme points. Could be errors or rare events.
No pattern = random scatter. Variables likely unrelated.
Always check for overplotting when many points overlap.
why_it_exists: Correlation coefficients (like Pearson's r) only detect linear relationships. A perfect U‑shape gives r near 0, but the relationship is strong. Scatter plots reveal the truth. They also show clustering and outliers that summary stats hide.
visual_alt: Gallery of 6 scatter plots: positive linear (orange), negative linear (yellow), U‑shape nonlinear (red), three color clusters (purple/green), one outlier as a red star, and random noise (blue).
when_to_use: Whenever you want to see relationship between two continuous variables.
Before calculating Pearson correlation – the plot tells you if linear is appropriate.
To spot clusters that could be different segments or groups.
To identify outliers that might be data errors.
common_mistakes: Relying on correlation without plotting. A U‑shape or outlier‑driven line can lie.
Ignoring overplotting – use transparency (alpha), hexbin plots, or sampling.
Claiming a nonlinear pattern is random just because correlation is near zero.
notes: Add a trend line (linear regression) to help the eye, but beware of forcing linearity.
For categorical vs continuous, use box plots or violin plots, not scatter.
ds_usage: Scatter plots are everywhere in EDA, diagnostic plots for regression (residuals vs fitted), and visualizing clustering results (PCA scatter plots). Also used in correlation heatmaps as a matrix of scatter plots.
